1352.title: The iconostasis
1352.hook: the Orthodox icon screen, both veil and window
1352.howItsDone: In Orthodox churches an iconostasis stands between the nave and the altar; worshipers light candles before its icons and venerate them, and the central doors open and close at set moments of the Divine Liturgy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the basilica: a Roman hall turned church, a long nave leading to a rounded apse. Your line was the long walk.

At the far end of an Orthodox church, right where the long walk would reach the altar, there's a wall. Not plain stone. A wall of faces. Christ on one side of a central doorway; on the other, Mary, holding him as a child. Angels on the side doors. Saints in rows, gold behind every head. Candles flicker, and in that light the faces seem to shift. Then, at a certain moment in the service, the central doors swing open: the altar, light, a priest moving. A little later, the doors close again. Today: the iconostasis.

The icon wars of day eight hundred one were fought over faces like these. The iconostasis is the screen of icons between the nave, where the people are, and the sanctuary, where the altar is. Orthodox Christians describe it two ways at once. First, a veil. In the temple in Jerusalem, a veil hung before the holiest place. Matthew says that when Jesus died, "behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom." So the screen still marks a threshold: something holy is behind it, and it isn't simply put on display. Second, a window. In the Orthodox understanding an icon isn't decoration. Colossians calls Christ "the image of the invisible God," and the Greek word there for image is eikon. Orthodox Christians teach that because God became visible in Christ, his face may be painted, and an icon opens onto the one it shows. So the congregation isn't facing a wall. It's facing a crowd: Christ, Mary, the saints, looking back. Third, the doors. The central ones, called the royal or holy doors, open and close during the liturgy. The gospel book passes through them. At communion, the cup is brought out through them. Hidden, then shown, then hidden. Paul put that rhythm into one sentence: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Other churches arrange this space in other ways, some with the altar in full view. The Orthodox screen holds both halves of Paul's line in one wall.
screen: `A WINDOW: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.`
`THROUGH A GLASS, DARKLY; THEN FACE TO FACE.`

If you pray, say Paul's words quietly, now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face, or simply let the face look back at you while you breathe.

1353.title: The gothic cathedral
1353.howItsDone: Gothic cathedrals across Europe, and gothic-style churches built since, are still used for daily and Sunday worship; visitors and worshipers alike walk the nave, look up into the vaults, and sit beneath the stained glass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iconostasis: the Orthodox wall of faces between the people and the altar. Your line was veil and window.

Stone wants to fall. Every block in a wall presses on the one below, and the higher a wall goes, the thicker its bottom has to be. Build big the plain way: heavy walls, small windows, a dim room. Then medieval builders tried another answer. They pointed their arches, so the weight ran down more steeply. They laid ribs of stone across the ceiling to gather the load into a few strong points. Outside, they threw arms of stone through the air, flying buttresses, to hold the walls up from beyond. Now the walls didn't carry everything. They could open up, and fill with colored glass.

A gothic cathedral does two things stone doesn't like to do: it rises high, and it lets light in. Some Christians have read both as more than engineering. Start with up. Walk in, and the columns run in thin lines from floor to vault, drawing the eye upward. A psalm says, "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." A gothic nave builds that sentence in stone: the whole room is a lifted gaze. Then, light. Much of the glass wasn't clear. It was colored, set with scenes from the Bible, prophets, the life of Jesus, the saints, for people below to look up and see. John's Gospel begins with light: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." On a gray morning, the light comes in already full of stories. Third, the stones. The first letter of Peter turns the picture around and says the building is people: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house." Lively, in the old English, means living. So a cathedral points past itself to a congregation, each person a stone, set beside the others and holding them up. Last, the labor. These were slow buildings, raised by masons, glaziers and carpenters. Psalm 127 puts that work in its place: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it." Stone, lifted toward light, and a psalm that names another builder.

Wherever you are, a church, a stairwell, or just under your own ceiling, let your eyes start at the floor and climb slowly, the way the eye climbs a column, to the highest point you can see, and rest them there. If you pray, say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. If not, just keep your eyes up.

1354.title: The plain meeting house
1354.hook: Quaker and Puritan rooms of white walls and clear glass
1354.howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, people gather in a plain room and sit in silence, and anyone may rise to speak when moved; churches in the Puritan and Reformed line gather in plain rooms centered on the reading and preaching of the Bible.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gothic cathedral: stone lifted high, walls turned into colored glass. Your line was stone reaching up.

White walls. Clear glass. Wooden benches. No statues, no painted windows, no altar. In a Quaker meeting house the benches may face each other, with no pulpit at all. People come in, sit down, and the room goes quiet. A clock ticks. Outside, a branch moves. After a while, someone stands, says a few sentences, and sits down. In an old New England meeting house built by Puritans, the room is just as bare, but everything turns toward a high pulpit where the Bible is read and preached. Two plain rooms, built that way on purpose.

Yesterday's cathedral asked how a building can lift the eye toward God. The meeting house, from the same Bible, asks what might stand in the way. Start with the building. In Athens, Paul tells a crowd standing among temples: "God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands." Plain builders leaned hard on that line. The room shelters the people, and that's its job. Next, the worship. Jesus tells a Samaritan woman at a well, "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Puritans wanted worship stripped back to what they found in scripture, so the Bible, read and preached, stands at the center. Quakers went another way into the same plainness. As day two hundred seventy-nine told, they speak of the light of Christ within each person, and they hear it in John's Gospel: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." So in a Quaker meeting of the silent kind, anyone may rise and speak, and no one has to. Then, the people: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In this reading, the gathering is the room's holy center. Last, the clear glass. No saints in the window, just the real sky and the real tree. On the mountain, Elijah learns that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. After the fire came "a still small voice."
screen: `DWELLETH NOT IN TEMPLES MADE WITH HANDS.`

segments.voice: Find the barest spot you can, a blank wall or an empty table, and sit with nothing to look at and nothing to do, letting thoughts pass. If you pray, wait the way a Quaker meeting waits, without asking for anything, listening for a still small voice. If you don't, sit in the quiet and let the plainness be enough.
The plain meeting house. A room kept bare on purpose, so that nothing stands between the gathered people and God.
Your line: nothing between. Just the gathered people, the quiet, and the real sky. Until tomorrow.

1355.title: Domes
1355.hook: the dome as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator looking down
1355.howItsDone: In Orthodox churches built with a central dome, the dome is painted as the heavens, in some with Christ Pantocrator at its height, and worshipers stand beneath it during the Divine Liturgy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plain meeting house: white walls, clear glass, a room kept bare on purpose. Your line was nothing between.

Over the center of some Orthodox churches, the ceiling doesn't stop. It curves up and closes into a dome, and from its very top a face looks down. Christ, painted large, one hand raised in blessing, the other holding a book. Around him, in some churches, angels circle; lower down, prophets and apostles; lower still, the walls with their saints; and at the bottom, the people, standing, heads tipped back. Stand right under the center and the whole building seems to turn around that one face, the way the sky seems to turn around wherever you stand. Today: domes.

A dome is a round roof. In an Orthodox church, it's also a picture of the sky. Isaiah describes God as the one "that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in." A tent over the whole earth. A dome builds that tent over one congregation: a curved heaven, with everyone underneath at once. Then, what the sky says: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm hears the real sky talking. A painted dome makes it easier to hear: instead of clouds, faces, and the highest is Christ. That image has a name: Christ Pantocrator. It's a Greek word from the New Testament itself. In Revelation, the Lord says: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty." The Almighty, in the Greek, is pantokrator. So the face at the top of the dome is the one Revelation calls the beginning and the end, blessing with one hand, holding the gospel book with the other. Last, the order of the room. Heaven at the top, earth at the bottom, and the walls between full of people who have lived on both. Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as heaven and earth worshiping together. Under a dome, the Lord's Prayer can be heard almost as a description of the room: "Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." In that picture, heaven isn't far off up there.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`
`IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.`

1356.title: Table, pulpit, font
1356.hook: where the furniture sits says what's central
1356.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches place the altar at the center; some Reformed and Presbyterian churches center the pulpit and the open Bible; some Baptist churches set the baptistry where the whole congregation can see it; other churches balance all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, domes: a round roof painted as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator looking down. Your line was heaven overhead.

A table. A pulpit. A font. Those three keep turning up in churches. In one church, the table stands in the middle at the front, candles on it, and the pulpit waits off to one side. In another, a tall pulpit rises dead center, a big Bible open on it, and the table sits lower down, in front. In a third, behind the pulpit, set high into the wall where everyone can see it, there's a pool of water deep enough to stand in. Three arrangements, and none of them by accident.

Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." A church's floor plan is a little like that: where the furniture stands shows what the people treasure in their worship. Start with the table. At the last supper, Jesus took bread and said, "This do in remembrance of me." Paul calls it "the Lord's table." Catholic Christians call it an altar, Orthodox Christians the holy table or altar, and they place it at the heart of the church, because they understand the Eucharist celebrated there as the center of their worship. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches do the same. Next, the pulpit. Paul writes, "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." In Reformed and Presbyterian churches, the pulpit may stand at the center with the Bible open on it, because the word read and preached is where they hear God speak. The table is still there, and honored, but the eye goes first to the open book. Then, the font: water for baptism. In some Baptist churches the baptistry, a pool for full immersion, is set high behind the pulpit, so every baptism happens in front of the whole room. Tomorrow, the font gets a day of its own. Last, all three together. Some churches set them in a line or a triangle, holding all three together. Every arrangement answers the same question in wood and stone instead of words. Christians don't all give the same answer, and each answer can be read from the back pew.

Let your eyes move around the room you're in without judging anything: what stands in the middle, and what do the chairs face, a table, a screen, a window? Rest your eyes on that center for a while. If you pray, hold Jesus's words in mind, where your treasure is, there will your heart be also; or simply notice what the room has been built around.

1357.title: The font at the door
1357.hook: some churches put the font by the door: you enter by baptism
1357.howItsDone: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door and make the sign of the cross as they enter; in some churches the baptismal font itself stands near the entrance, while others baptize at the front or in a river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, table, pulpit, font: where a church puts its furniture shows what it puts first. Your line was what's at the center.

Rain on her coat, a woman comes in off the street. Two steps in, her hand goes out to a small stone basin fixed to the wall. She dips her fingertips, touches her forehead, her chest, one shoulder, the other, and walks on without breaking stride. Behind her, a father lifts a small boy up so he can reach the water too. In other churches, the big font itself, where people are baptized, stands just inside the entrance, so everyone who comes in walks past it. Water first. Then the rest of the church.

Some churches put the font at the door for one reason: in Christian teaching, a person enters the church by baptism. Start with the entrance. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus, "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Enter is the word, so the water sits where you enter. Next, the meaning. Paul describes baptism as a burial: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Down into the water, up out of it, and then you walk. With the font by the door, every walk up the aisle starts beside that water. Then, the door. Jesus says, "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved." A font beside the door puts the two pictures side by side. Last, the fingertips. Catholics dip their fingers in holy water on the way in and make the sign of the cross. Some describe it as a reminder, every time, of their baptism. Not every church places its water at the entrance. Some baptize at the front, before the whole congregation, and some in a river. As day one hundred fifty-two showed, Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches baptize infants; Baptists and some others baptize those old enough to speak their own faith. Different doors, the same water.

1358.title: Bells
1358.hook: bells call to prayer, toll for death, ring for joy
1358.howItsDone: Churches ring bells to call people to services and to prayer, toll them slowly at funerals, and ring them in celebration at weddings and feasts; in Catholic tradition the Angelus bell rings at set hours, and the bells fall silent from Holy Thursday until the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the font at the door: water at the entrance, because a Christian enters the church by baptism. Your line was enter by water.

Noon in a small town. A bell rings out over the rooftops. Nobody sent a text, but a woman in a shop doorway glances up, and an old man lowers his newspaper. Another day, the same bell rings slowly: one stroke, then a long gap, then another. People on the street go quiet, because they know what that means. Someone has died. And another day, every bell in the tower goes at once, and a wedding party spills into the sunlight. One tower, three messages, and the whole town reads them without a word.

Church bells do three jobs. Start with Exodus, where the high priest's robe has golden bells along its hem, between pomegranates of colored thread. Why bells? "His sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD." A bell announces that someone is coming before God, and a church bell carries a sound like that out to a whole town. First job: the call to prayer. In Catholic tradition, the Angelus bell rings at set hours of the day, and people stop and pray where they are. Orthodox ringers strike patterns for the services and feasts. Second job: the toll for death, a slow bell for someone who has died. The poet and preacher John Donne, lying sick and hearing a church bell toll for someone else, wrote that we should never send to ask who it's for, because it tolls for us as well: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." In Donne's reading, this death belongs to all of us. Third job: joy. Weddings. Easter. In Catholic churches, the bells fall silent on Holy Thursday and come back ringing at the Easter Vigil. The prophet Zechariah even pictures a day when holiness reaches the ordinary bells: "In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD." Put the three together and you hear Paul: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." A bell does both, out loud, for everyone in earshot.

Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen outward, past the room, for anything that rings or chimes, a clock, a bike, a spoon against a glass, or whatever is farthest away. If you pray, hold one person in mind for each sound you hear. When the bell comes at the end, let it ring all the way out before you move.
Bells. A church tower's voice: they call to prayer, toll for the dead, and ring for joy, so a whole town hears.
Your line: for whom it tolls. Joy and grief, rung out for everyone. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why does that church bell sometimes ring slowly, just one bong at a time?
options: A slow toll marks a death; bells also call people to prayer and ring out for joy.
It means the bell is broken; a working bell always rings fast for every service.
It means the church is closed today; a slow bell tells people to stay home.
chat.meaning: A slow toll is for someone who has died. Bells also call to prayer and ring for joy, weeping and rejoicing out loud for the whole town.
